svg.text: Address-space layout — heap ↑ · stack ↓ meet at the gap
one process’s virtual address space — six regions in a fixed order; the program’s own calls move the two boundaries toward each other
STEP 1/5 · ACT 0 — load null · text · data
STEP 3/5 · ACT 2 — mmap libc into gap
STEP 5/5 · ACT 4 — sp plunges into gap
heap / gap / stack: reserved, still empty
malloc(Δ): brk += Δ — edge only rises
call f(): sp −= 0x40 — pointer only falls
f() calls f() forever — no base case
each call: sp −= 0x40, again and again
⋮ sp plunges past the stack band ⋮
next touch lands in the gap — unmapped
uniform band heights — not to scale (axis spans ~47 bits ≈ 128 TB)
Schematic: uniform band heights, NOT to scale — the address axis spans ~47 bits (~128 TB);
the gap dwarfs every named region. ASLR: the kernel randomizes each region’s start every run;
the order and permissions drawn here never change. Invariant: heap and stack may each grow
arbitrarily far, but the layout’s job is to keep the two from silently overwriting each other.
Security: code is R+X never W; data/heap/stack are R+W never X — no region grants both, so
injected bytes can never execute. A null pointer (0x0) always faults — the null page is unmapped.
Symmetric failure (not drawn): a heap that never frees climbs up through the gap — same collision.
Each process has its own private copy of this layout (virtual memory); the page table enforces
per-region R/W/X — that is why an unmapped touch faults instead of silently succeeding.
↺ in a stage box = the loop repeats
